summary.text:
Merseyside Fire and Rescue Authority's 2025/26 Treasury Management Annual Report went to Audit Committee on 30 June 2026. Five-page covering report plus six-page Appendix A carrying all the figures. Read together. The Authority's treasury function is delivered by Liverpool City Council under an SLA (cost £28,807 in 2025/26). Report author is Mike Rea, Director of Finance and Procurement — the Authority's s151. No officer email addresses in either paper.

The reconciliation is the cleanest we have seen. Our file holds 26 PWLB loans totalling £33,720,000 at a weighted 5.0857%, tying the paper's £33.720m external debt at 31 March 2026 to the penny. Because no new loans were taken and none repaid, the £1.715m interest paid over the year works back to 5.086% — one basis point off our engine's snapshot weighted rate. And the paper's maturity table shows 100% of the book in the 10-years-and-above bucket for the whole year; our file splits the same 26 loans as 7 in 10-25y and 19 in 25y+, with nothing in any shorter bucket. Three separate ties on the same £33.720m book.

Balance-sheet identity ties at every year-end printed. CFR less external borrowing less PFI equals under-borrowing at 31/3/2025 (0.3), 31/3/2026 (7.5) and 31/3/2027 estimate (13.0). The Authority is running a deliberate deferral of new long-term borrowing — cover para 15 says explicitly that available cash balances are funding capital expenditure 'at a time when investment returns remain relatively low compared to borrowing costs', and Appendix A para 7 confirms new LT borrowing was envisaged for 2025/26 but 'no new long-term borrowing was arranged given the unfavourable environment'. Under-borrowing widens £12.7m over two years as the CFR grows and external debt stays flat. The next borrowing question comes into view in the 12–24 months to the 2026/27 outturn.

Maturity shape is the unusual bit sector-wide. 100% at 10+ years is a shape no other council in our library carries — most report material principal in the under-2-year buckets. The book has no refinancing pressure at all inside the plan period. Interest rate exposure is 100% fixed / 0% variable against limits of 100%/50% — a static, fully-fixed, wholly-PWLB book.

Email drafted around three findings: the exact reconciliation (26 loans / £33.720m / 5.0857% against £33.720m external debt and £1.715m interest paid), the long-only maturity shape (100% at 10+ years is genuinely rare), and the widening under-borrowing trajectory that turns into a borrowing decision inside the next twelve months if the CFR path is right. Meeting has passed so the send-by targets the H2 2026/27 interim report. Draft not sendable until an officer email is confirmed — no address is printed in either paper.

officer.body:
Hi Mike,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every authority's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, the inter-LA lending market, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council and every fire authority in the country, so we can see how a body's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Treasury Management Annual Report that went to Audit Committee on 30 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Before anything else, your report let us check ourselves. Our file for you holds 26 PWLB loans totalling £33,720,000 at a weighted 5.0857%, which ties your Appendix A page 4 external debt line at £33.720m to the penny. And because you took no new loans and none matured in the year (cover para 15), your £1.715m of interest paid across the year works back to 5.0860% — one basis point off our snapshot. Your maturity table also prints 100% of the book at 10+ years, and our file agrees: 7 loans in 10-25 years for £8.5m and 19 loans in 25+ years for £25.2m, with nothing shorter. Three separate cross-checks on the same book, all tying. That's a useful thing to be able to write down.

The shape itself is worth flagging separately. Across the reports we've read this year, a 100% long-only book is the exception rather than the rule — most authorities carry material principal in the under-two-year buckets and are working through refinancing decisions there. Yours has no refinancing pressure inside the plan period at all. Combined with the 100%-fixed exposure in your para 14a (against a 50% variable ceiling), it's genuinely one of the more stable positions we've seen.

The decision that comes into view instead is on the CFR path. Your page 4 table has under-borrowing at 0.3, 7.5 and 13.0 across the three year-ends, with external debt held flat at £33.7m by choice. Cover para 15 is explicit about why — cash balances funding capital 'at a time when investment returns remain relatively low compared to borrowing costs' — and Appendix A para 7 says the environment was unfavourable enough that the new long-term borrowing you had envisaged for 2025/26 wasn't taken. That call was made against a year in which the 25-year PWLB ranged 5.78% to 6.43% (your own page 2 table). Today the 25-year certainty rate is around 6.46% — right at the year-high your table records. So the environment that prompted the deferral hasn't materially improved, and if the £13.0m estimate at 31 March 2027 is the right shape then the borrowing question sits inside the twelve months to the outturn rather than beyond it. The monthly picture of what the sector is actually paying is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%.

One standing note. CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of every member. Yours isn't printed in this annual report but is the kind of thing an Audit Committee member is likely to ask about at the next interim or the next annual strategy. We hold an interactive version fed by live rates so the shape moves as the market does — worth a look if it isn't a chart your Liverpool colleagues currently produce for you.

On training, four fit the position the report describes. PWLB drawdown mechanics — certainty vs standard rate becomes live the moment the 2026/27 borrowing question turns from deferral to action. Cost of carry and internal borrowing goes to the CFR-vs-external-debt gap that the under-borrowing figure represents. Liability benchmark — reading it and setting one connects to the CIPFA point above. And Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee your annual report was just heard by. All 115 courses are free to fire authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others — inside the Authority or across your Liverpool contacts — would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management 2025/26 Annual Report (report DFP/02/2627 plus Appendix A), Audit Committee, 30 June 2026 (mfra.merseyfire.gov.uk documents s35777 and s35778).
